newsitem.title: USA: HK to stay top financial center - China cenbanker.
newsitem.headline: HK to stay top financial center - China cenbanker.

text.p: With 137 days to go before Hong Kong reverts to China, top Chinese and Hong Kong central bankers reassured U.S. investors on Friday that Hong Kong will remain the region's pre-eminent financial center.

A Chinese central bank deputy governor said that Hong Kong will long overshadow its closest potential competitor, Shanghai, because China has no timetable yet to make its currency, the Renminbi, convertible.

"At least before the Renminbi becomes fully convertible, Shanghai does not possess the prerequisites to become an international financial center," said Chen Yuan, Deputy Governor of People's Bank of China, at a seminar at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York on Friday.
Joseph Yam, chief executive of Hong Kong Monetary Authority, also told the seminar that Hong Kong's "robust financial infrastructure" would ensure its status as a global financial center.

Chen said Hong Kong will continue to maintain its own independent system of currency issuance and management, and the Hong Kong dollar will continue to be fixed at 7.80 per U.S. dollar in a currency board system which has been in place since 1983.

As spelled out in a bilateral repurchase agreement of U.S. Treasury securities in February 1996, Beijing will stand by to help Hong Kong to defend its currency when needed, said Chen, whose father Chen Yun was a revolutionary leader who backed limited economic reform.
China's foreign exchange reserves of US$105 billion, which are the largest in the world after Japan.

Yam, whose monetary authority is Hong Kong's de facto central bank, told the seminar it is unlikely that Hong Kong would need hlp from mainland China to fend off speculators since it has US$80 billion of reserves of its own.

To maintain Hong Kong's competitive edge as a financial center, Yam highlighted the territory's recent advances, including a new payment and settlement system for banks introduced last December which is known as the Hong Kong's Real Time Gross Settlement (RTGS) system.
Yam underscored that the Heritage Foundation, a conservative U.S. think tank, ranks Hong Kong as the freest economy in the world for three years in a row.
Chief executives of top Hong Kong banks also expressed confidence that Hong Kong would remain a major financial center after the territory reverts to China on July 1, 1997.
Wang Xuebing, chairman and president of Beijing-owned Bank of China, emphasized that Hong Kong will continue playing a major role in raising capital for mainland China.

Foreign investors prefer a simultaneous listing in Hong Kong even if the stocks of a Chinese enterprise are listed on the one of their markets, he said, pointing to the example of Shanghai Petrochemical 600688.S, which is listed in Hong Kong and New York.
"Hong Kong is the information hub for all aspects of mainland China market," he said.
John Bond, Group Chief Executive of HSBC Holdings Plc, and Patrick Gillam, chairman of Standard Chartered Bank both said the economy would be run in the post-transition period much as it is now.
Whatever difficulties Hong Kong may encounter in the transition, they would be overcome in the "usual prgramatic Hong Kong way," Bond said.
About 280 people from the investment community and the media attended the seminar, moderated by Nnew York Fred President William McDonough.
